Regarding your question about why code might fail in the context of LLM applications, it is helpful to understand the difference between traditional software and LLM-based systems. As we discuss in the course, traditional software is deterministic, meaning that if you provide the same input, you will consistently receive the same output. For example, a login function is designed to be deterministic: if the credentials are correct, the login succeeds, and if they are incorrect, it fails.

In contrast, LLM-based applications are probabilistic. This means that even with the same input, you might receive different outputs. When building and evaluating these systems, we focus on ensuring quality—such as correctness and accuracy—because, unlike a simple calculator, LLMs can hallucinate or provide incorrect information. To manage this, we use techniques like benchmarking (using libraries like the one from EleutherAI) and continuous monitoring in production to identify failures, which we then use to update our "golden data set" to improve the system over time.

testCases.name: test_case_4
testCases.input: My name is Anjali and I am studying the LLM evals course. What is the difference between model evals and application evals?
testCases.actualOutput:
Hello Anjali! It is great to have you in the course. Understanding the distinction between these two types of evaluations is a perfect place to start.

To keep things simple, we categorize LLM evaluations into two types: model evals and application evals. While the industry often refers to both simply as "LLM evals," making this distinction helps clarify the goal of your testing.

**Model evals** are focused on evaluating the LLM itself. The primary goal here is to test and document the inherent capabilities of a model—such as its reasoning, mathematical ability, or general knowledge—often when a new model is released. You can think of this as checking the "brain" of the system. These are typically done in two ways: through standardized benchmarks (generic datasets used to compare models on leaderboards) or through custom model evals, where you test a model against your own specific data to see if it is the right fit for your needs.

**Application evals**, on the other hand, are used to evaluate LLM-based applications. Instead of just testing the model's raw capability, you are assessing how well the entire system performs within the context of the specific application you are building. 

In short, model evals are about understanding the performance of the underlying model, while application evals are about ensuring your specific LLM-powered system works as intended. We focus more heavily on application evals in this course, as they are essential for verifying that your final product meets its requirements.
